title: Hamersley banded iron formations peak
summary: Vast layered iron-oxide deposits accumulate in the Hamersley Basin of Western Australia, today among the world's largest sources of iron ore.
description: Banded iron formations, rocks of alternating iron-oxide and chert layers, were laid down in enormous volumes at the end of the Archean and start of the Proterozoic, notably in the Hamersley Basin of Western Australia and the Transvaal basin of South Africa. They record dissolved iron in a largely oxygen-poor ocean being oxidised and precipitated, at least partly by oxygen released by photosynthesising cyanobacteria, although the relative roles of oxygen, iron-oxidising microbes and other processes are still debated. Their deposition waned as the Great Oxidation Event changed the chemistry of the oceans and atmosphere, although banded iron formations returned in a major pulse around 1.88 billion years ago, notably in the Lake Superior region, and briefly again during the Cryogenian glaciations. These rocks now supply most of the world's iron ore.

title: Huronian glaciation
summary: At least three glacial episodes leave thick ice-laid deposits along the north shore of Lake Huron, among Earth's earliest major ice ages.
description: The Huronian Supergroup of Ontario contains three glacial diamictite units, the Ramsay Lake, Bruce and Gowganda formations, deposited between about 2.45 and 2.22 billion years ago, an interval bracketed by underlying volcanic rocks and the cross-cutting Nipissing intrusions. Broadly similar glacial deposits occur in the northern United States, Fennoscandia, South Africa and Western Australia, although their exact correlation is uncertain. Many researchers link the glaciations to the Great Oxidation Event, since rising oxygen would have destroyed atmospheric methane, a powerful greenhouse gas. Whether any of the episodes covered the whole planet, as a Paleoproterozoic 'Snowball Earth', remains debated.

title: Great Oxidation Event
summary: Oxygen made by cyanobacteria accumulates in the atmosphere for the first time, permanently transforming Earth's chemistry and the course of life.
description: During the early Paleoproterozoic, free oxygen rose from trace levels to perhaps 1–10 percent of today's concentration, as oxygen produced by photosynthesising cyanobacteria finally outpaced the volcanic gases and dissolved iron that had consumed it. The clearest marker is the disappearance of mass-independent sulfur isotope fractionation, which can only be preserved under an almost oxygen-free atmosphere; sections in South Africa's Transvaal Supergroup place this change at roughly 2.43–2.33 billion years ago. Oxidised soils and red beds appear, detrital grains of pyrite and uraninite vanish from river deposits, and the loss of methane may have helped trigger the Huronian glaciations. Recent studies suggest oxygen levels fluctuated for some 200 million years before stabilising, so the precise onset and end of the event are still being refined.

title: Makganyene glaciation: an early Snowball Earth?
summary: Glacial deposits in South Africa's Northern Cape are closely tied to lavas erupted near the equator, hinting that ice reached the tropics.
description: The Makganyene Formation of the Transvaal Supergroup contains glacial diamictite closely associated with the overlying Ongeluk lavas, whose preserved magnetisation indicates eruption at low latitude. If the two units are closely linked in time, ice reached sea level near the equator, which Joseph Kirschvink and colleagues proposed in 2000 as evidence for a Paleoproterozoic 'Snowball Earth'. Dating of the Ongeluk volcanics to about 2.43 billion years ago places the glaciation near the first rise of atmospheric oxygen and possibly in step with the Huronian glaciations of North America.
mainstreamView: Most geologists accept that the Makganyene diamictite is glacial and that the Ongeluk lavas erupted at low latitude, but whether the glaciation was truly global is unresolved. Its correlation with other Paleoproterozoic glacial units is uncertain, and earlier studies dated it to around 2.22 billion years ago, so its relationship to the Great Oxidation Event is still argued over.

title: Lomagundi–Jatuli carbon isotope excursion
summary: Marine carbonates worldwide record the largest and longest positive carbon-isotope excursion in Earth history, named after rocks in Zimbabwe and Karelia.
description: Carbonate rocks of this age, first described from the Lomagundi Group of Zimbabwe and the Jatulian rocks of Russian Karelia and Finland, are strongly enriched in carbon-13, with δ13C values often above +10‰. The anomaly is usually interpreted as a prolonged episode of unusually high burial of organic carbon, which would have released large amounts of oxygen and helped raise atmospheric oxygen during the later part of the Great Oxidation Event. Its cause, duration and global extent remain subjects of research, and many studies suggest it was followed by a decline in oxygen levels after about 2.06 billion years ago.

title: Francevillian biota of Gabon
summary: Centimetre-scale pyritised structures in Gabonese black shales are claimed as the oldest large colonial organisms, a contested interpretation.
description: In 2010 a team led by Moroccan geologist Abderrazak El Albani described more than 250 flattened, lobate structures up to 12 cm across from the Francevillian B Formation near Franceville, Gabon. The researchers interpreted them as colonial organisms living in newly oxygenated shallow seas after the Great Oxidation Event, possibly the earliest multicellular life, and later papers reported string-like trails suggestive of movement. The host shales are unusually well preserved and unmetamorphosed, but the biological nature of the structures has not been widely accepted.
mainstreamView: Many palaeontologists regard the Francevillian structures as pyrite concretions or microbial-mat features rather than true multicellular organisms, pointing to the lack of cellular detail. Widely accepted eukaryote fossils appear more than 400 million years later, so the Gabon finds remain an intriguing but contested claim.

title: Bushveld Igneous Complex forms
summary: Vast volumes of magma invade the crust of what is now South Africa, forming Earth's largest layered intrusion and richest store of platinum metals.
description: The Bushveld Igneous Complex, north of Pretoria, was intruded into the sedimentary rocks of the Transvaal Supergroup about 2.055 billion years ago, some 30 million years before the nearby Vredefort impact. It covers more than 66,000 square kilometres, about the area of Ireland, and its layered suite of mafic and ultramafic rocks reaches up to about 9 km thick, exposed in western, eastern and northern limbs around a broad basin. Repeated injections of magma that crystallised in thin, remarkably continuous layers concentrated metals into ore bodies such as the Merensky Reef and the chromite-rich UG2 layer. Together they hold about three-quarters of the world's known platinum resources and around half of its palladium, as well as most of its chromium reserves and large amounts of vanadium. The complex is generally attributed to mantle-derived magmas, possibly fed by a mantle plume, while how its ore layers formed is still actively debated.

title: Vredefort impact
summary: A large asteroid strikes what is now South Africa, blasting a crater perhaps 170–300 km wide, the largest known impact structure on Earth.
description: The Vredefort structure, centred near the town of Vredefort in Free State province, formed about 2.023 billion years ago (±4 million years). The original crater has long since eroded away, but its rebounded central uplift, the Vredefort Dome, still measures about 100–120 km across, and shatter cones and shocked quartz confirm its impact origin. Estimates of the original crater diameter range from about 170 to 300 km, implying an impactor commonly put at 10–15 km across, with some recent models favouring a larger body. The Vredefort Dome was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2005.

title: Svecofennian orogeny builds Fennoscandia
summary: Island arcs collide with the ancient Karelian craton, building much of the bedrock of present-day Finland and Sweden.
description: The Svecofennian orogeny was a series of mountain-building events in which volcanic island arcs and microcontinents accreted to the Archean Karelian craton, enlarging it from the northeast towards the southwest. The resulting granites, gneisses and volcanic rocks form much of the crust of central and southern Finland and Sweden, including the Central Finland Granitoid Complex. The orogeny was part of a worldwide episode of continental collisions between about 2.1 and 1.8 billion years ago that assembled the supercontinent Columbia, also called Nuna. Its eroded roots host important ore deposits, such as those of the Skellefteå district and the Bergslagen region around Falun.

title: Oklo natural nuclear reactors
summary: Groundwater-moderated chain reactions start up in uranium ore at Oklo, Gabon, the only known natural nuclear fission reactors.
description: In the Francevillian basin of Gabon, uranium ore reached critical conditions because natural uranium then contained about 3 percent fissile uranium-235, similar to modern reactor fuel, and groundwater acted as a neutron moderator. Sixteen reactor zones operated intermittently for a few hundred thousand years, apparently cycling on and off as water boiled away and seeped back. The reactors were discovered in 1972 after French analysts noticed that uranium from the Oklo mine was depleted in uranium-235. Published estimates of when they operated range from about 2.0 to 1.7 billion years ago, and the site is studied as a natural analogue for long-term nuclear waste storage and as a test of whether fundamental physical constants have changed.

title: Oklo as an artificial 'ancient reactor'
summary: Ancient-astronaut writers claim the Oklo reactors in Gabon were built by a lost prehistoric civilisation or by visitors from space.
description: Popular ancient-astronaut and alternative-history books, websites and television programmes have presented the Oklo reactors as a two-billion-year-old nuclear power plant or waste dump left by a vanished civilisation or extraterrestrial visitors. Proponents argue that a self-sustaining chain reaction is too improbable to have arisen naturally and point to how stably the reactors appear to have operated. The claim is not supported by any physical artefact or peer-reviewed scientific study.
mainstreamView: Natural reactors were predicted from basic physics by chemist Paul Kuroda in 1956, years before Oklo was found: billions of years ago uranium contained enough uranium-235 to sustain fission when moderated by groundwater. Isotopic analyses of xenon, neodymium and other fission products at Oklo match this natural, self-regulating process, the reactor zones are irregular ore lenses within sedimentary rock, and no tools, structures or other traces of engineering have ever been found. Life on Earth at the time was almost entirely microbial.

title: Gunflint chert microfossils
summary: Black chert on Lake Superior's north shore preserves a diverse community of microbes, the first Precambrian cellular fossils to be widely accepted.
description: The Gunflint Iron Formation, a banded iron formation exposed along the north shore of Lake Superior in northwestern Ontario and neighbouring Minnesota, contains layers of black chert with exceptionally preserved microscopic fossils inside stromatolites. Geologist Stanley Tyler collected the chert near Schreiber, Ontario, in 1953, and with palaeobotanist Elso Barghoorn he reported its fossils in 1954, followed by a full description in 1965. The assemblage includes filaments and spheres such as Gunflintia and Huroniospora and the star-shaped Eoastrion, interpreted as cyanobacteria, iron- or manganese-oxidising bacteria and other microbes. It was the first widely accepted evidence of cellular life in Precambrian rocks and helped launch the study of early life, and although older microfossils are now known it remains one of the most diverse early microbial communities. Volcanic ash in the formation has been dated to about 1.88 billion years ago, during a worldwide pulse of banded iron deposition.

title: Sudbury impact
summary: A large impact in what is now Ontario creates the Sudbury structure, whose solidified melt sheet hosts some of the world's richest nickel ores.
description: About 1.849 billion years ago a bolide perhaps 10–15 km across struck the southern margin of the Superior craton, forming a crater estimated at roughly 130–200 km wide. Later mountain building squeezed the structure into the elliptical Sudbury Basin, about 60 km long and 30 km wide. The impact melted a vast volume of crust, and the resulting Sudbury Igneous Complex concentrated nickel, copper and platinum-group metals that have been mined since the 1880s. Shatter cones and impact breccias confirm its origin, and some researchers have suggested the impactor was a comet rather than an asteroid.

title: Supercontinent Columbia (Nuna)
summary: Collisions such as the Trans-Hudson orogeny weld most continental blocks into Columbia, often regarded as Earth's first true supercontinent.
description: Columbia, also called Nuna or Hudsonland, was assembled through global-scale collisions between about 2.1 and 1.8 billion years ago, including the Trans-Hudson orogeny that stitched together the Archean cratons of North America. Its core is thought to have joined Laurentia, Baltica, the Ukrainian Shield, Amazonia and Australia, with Siberia, North China and the Kalahari craton possibly attached. It continued to grow by accretion along its margins before fragmenting between about 1.5 and 1.3 billion years ago. The supercontinent was proposed in 2002 by John Rogers and M. Santosh, and its precise configuration, reconstructed from palaeomagnetic and geological correlations, is still debated.

title: The 'Boring Billion'
summary: A billion years of relative environmental stability, low oxygen and slow evolutionary change follows the Great Oxidation Event.
description: The informal 'Boring Billion', also called Earth's Middle Ages, spans roughly 1.8 to 0.8 billion years ago, between the Great Oxidation Event and the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event. Atmospheric oxygen appears to have stayed low, the deep ocean was largely anoxic and in places sulfidic (a so-called Canfield ocean, documented in rocks such as those of the McArthur Basin in northern Australia), carbon isotopes were remarkably steady, and there is no firm evidence of glaciation. Eukaryotes nonetheless originated and slowly diversified during this time, including the first multicellular algae and the earliest evidence of sexual reproduction. Researchers increasingly stress that the interval also saw major tectonic events, such as the break-up of Columbia and the assembly of Rodinia, so its 'boring' reputation is partly a matter of perspective.

title: Mitochondria arise through endosymbiosis
summary: An archaeal cell acquires a bacterial partner whose descendants become mitochondria, the energy-producing organelles of complex cells.
description: Genetic evidence shows that mitochondria descend from free-living alphaproteobacteria that came to live inside an archaeal host cell, a partnership at the root of all eukaryotes. The closest known archaeal relatives of eukaryotes, the Asgard archaea, were first identified in 2015 from sediments near the Loki's Castle hydrothermal vents in the Arctic Ocean, the spot used to represent this event. The energy supplied by mitochondria may have allowed eukaryotic cells to support much larger genomes and more complex internal structures. The timing is poorly constrained: the event must predate the last eukaryotic common ancestor, which already had mitochondria, but molecular-clock estimates vary widely, and whether the nucleus or the mitochondrion came first is still debated.

title: First eukaryotes: complex cells appear
summary: Microfossils from North China show that complex cells with nuclei, ancestors of plants, animals and fungi, existed by about 1.65 billion years ago.
description: Eukaryotes, cells with a nucleus and internal organelles, are the lineage that later gave rise to all plants, animals and fungi. The oldest widely accepted eukaryotic fossils include ornamented acritarchs and multicellular filaments from the Chuanlinggou Formation of North China, about 1.64 billion years old, with similar forms such as Tappania appearing in India and Australia over the following 150 million years. Older candidates, including the 1.87-billion-year-old coiled fossil Grypania and the 2.1-billion-year-old Francevillian structures, are disputed, and steroid biomarkers once reported from 2.7-billion-year-old Australian rocks were later shown to be contamination. Molecular clocks give a wide range of dates for the origin of the group.
mainstreamView: Most palaeontologists accept that eukaryotes were present by about 1.65–1.6 billion years ago, based on wall ornamentation and cell structures that bacteria do not produce. When the lineage first arose is genuinely uncertain: molecular clocks and disputed older fossils allow an origin before 1.8 billion years ago, while biomarker studies suggest that modern (crown-group) eukaryotes became ecologically prominent only after about 800 million years ago.

title: Rafatazmia: possible 1.6-billion-year-old red algae
summary: Filamentous fossils from India's Vindhyan rocks are described as red algae, which would make them the oldest known members of a living group.
description: In 2017 Stefan Bengtson and colleagues described three-dimensionally preserved filaments (Rafatazmia) and lobed thalli (Ramathallus) from phosphorite in the Tirohan Dolomite near Chitrakoot, central India, dated to about 1.6 billion years ago. Cellular structures and growth patterns that they compared with those of modern red algae led them to interpret the fossils as crown-group red algae. If correct, they would be more than 500 million years older than Bangiomorpha and would push back the origin of photosynthetic eukaryotes considerably.
mainstreamView: The fossils are accepted as genuine and very old, but their identification as true red algae is contested because the diagnostic features are open to other interpretations, including cyanobacteria. Many molecular-clock studies place the origin of red algae well after 1.6 billion years ago, so most researchers still treat Bangiomorpha, about 1.05 billion years old, as the oldest securely identified red alga.

title: Ornamented acritarchs of the Roper Group
summary: Shales of northern Australia's Roper Group preserve spiny and ornamented acritarchs, early single-celled eukaryotes with complex cell walls.
description: Acritarchs are organic-walled microfossils of uncertain affinity, many of them probably the resting cysts of single-celled algae. In mudstones of the Roper Group, Northern Territory, about 1.5 billion years old, Emmanuelle Javaux and colleagues documented forms such as Tappania, with irregular tubular processes, and Valeria, with finely striated walls, whose construction implies a cytoskeleton and membrane system found only in eukaryotes. Their distribution from shallow to deeper-water settings suggests that eukaryotes were established, though not yet abundant, members of mid-Proterozoic marine ecosystems. Acritarch diversity remained modest through the Boring Billion before rising sharply in the Neoproterozoic.

title: Burdick's 'Precambrian pollen' in the Grand Canyon
dateLabel: c. 1.2 billion years ago (age of the rocks; claim made in 1966)
summary: Creationist Clifford Burdick reports conifer and flowering-plant pollen in the Grand Canyon's Precambrian Hakatai Shale as evidence against evolution.
description: In 1966 Clifford Burdick, a young-Earth creationist, reported in the Creation Research Society Quarterly that samples of the Hakatai Shale, part of the Grand Canyon's Unkar Group, contained pollen and spores of conifers, Ephedra, members of the daisy family and other seed plants. Because seed plants are otherwise unknown before the Devonian Period, more than 800 million years later, he and other creationists presented the find as evidence that the conventional fossil sequence and geological time scale are wrong. Burdick published further samples in 1972 that he said confirmed his results, and the claim still circulates in creationist literature as an out-of-place fossil.
mainstreamView: Pollen is abundant in the modern environment and easily contaminates rock samples during collection and laboratory processing, or by seeping into cracks. Beginning in 1971, Arthur Chadwick, himself a creationist researcher, collected about fifty samples from the same formation under strict contamination controls and found no authentic pollen, concluding in 1981 that Burdick's grains were modern contaminants. Burdick's grains were also never shown to have the darkening and alteration expected of genuinely ancient pollen, and the Hakatai Shale, about 1.25–1.1 billion years old, records no other trace of land plants.

title: Midcontinent Rift nearly splits North America
summary: A 2,000 km rift tears into the heart of ancestral North America around Lake Superior, pouring out vast basalt floods before failing to open an ocean.
description: About 1.1 billion years ago the interior of Laurentia, the ancestral core of North America, began to pull apart along a rift about 2,000 km long, curving from Kansas through the Lake Superior region and south into Michigan. Over roughly 20 million years enormous volumes of basalt lava erupted into the subsiding rift, accumulating to many kilometres thick beneath Lake Superior, while large intrusions such as the Duluth Complex formed nearby. The rift stopped widening before a new ocean could open, probably in part because compression from the Grenville orogeny on Laurentia's eastern margin squeezed it shut. Its Keweenawan rocks host the native copper of Michigan's Keweenaw Peninsula and Isle Royale, worked by Indigenous peoples for thousands of years and mined industrially from the 1840s, and its buried basalts produce a strong gravity anomaly across the American Midwest.

title: Supercontinent Rodinia
summary: Grenville-age collisions gather most continents into Rodinia, a supercontinent centred on Laurentia, the ancestral core of North America.
description: Rodinia, from the Russian for 'motherland', assembled through collisions between about 1.3 and 0.9 billion years ago, recorded worldwide in Grenville-age mountain belts, and was largely complete by around 1 billion years ago. Most reconstructions place Laurentia at its centre, surrounded by Baltica, Amazonia, Australia, East Antarctica and other blocks. Rifting began around 800–750 million years ago and continued for well over 100 million years, opening the proto-Pacific Ocean; the associated outpourings of basalt and changes in weathering have been linked to the onset of the Sturtian Snowball Earth. Because palaeomagnetism constrains ancient latitude but not longitude, Rodinia's exact configuration remains debated.

title: Grenville orogeny
summary: A Himalayan-scale continental collision along eastern Laurentia raises mountains from Labrador to Mexico during the assembly of Rodinia.
description: The Grenville orogeny, named after the village of Grenville in Quebec, records the collision of Laurentia with Amazonia and other blocks as Rodinia formed. Its main phases, the Ottawan (about 1.09–1.02 billion years ago) and the Rigolet (about 1.01–0.98 billion years ago), followed earlier Grenvillian events from around 1.25 billion years ago. The deeply eroded roots of the mountain belt, exposed as high-grade gneisses of the Grenville Province and the Adirondack Mountains, extend from Labrador to Mexico and have counterparts in Scotland, southwest Scandinavia (the Sveconorwegian orogen), Brazil and Africa. Grenville-age rocks form the basement beneath much of eastern North America.

title: Bangiomorpha: oldest known sexual reproduction
summary: A red alga from Arctic Canada with specialised reproductive cells is the oldest widely accepted fossil evidence of sex and of a living eukaryote group.
description: Bangiomorpha pubescens, described by Nicholas Butterfield in 2000 from silicified tidal-flat deposits of the Hunting Formation on Somerset Island, Nunavut, closely resembles the living red alga Bangia. Its multicellular filaments contain distinct reproductive cells interpreted as spores and gametes, making it the oldest known evidence of sexual reproduction and of complex multicellularity in a taxonomically resolved organism. Rhenium–osmium dating of the host rocks published in 2018 placed the fossils at about 1.047 billion years old, younger than earlier estimates of around 1.2 billion years. As the oldest securely identified member of a living group, Bangiomorpha anchors many molecular-clock estimates for the evolution of eukaryotes and photosynthetic plastids.

title: Tonian diversification of eukaryotes
summary: Algae, early fungi-like forms and the first shelled protists spread through Tonian seas, preserved in rocks such as the Grand Canyon's Chuar Group.
description: The Tonian, the first period of the Neoproterozoic Era (1,000–720 million years ago), saw a marked rise in the diversity of eukaryotic microfossils. Some of the oldest known green algae and possible fungi appear and red algae diversify, while the Chuar Group of the eastern Grand Canyon, roughly 780–730 million years old, contains vase-shaped microfossils interpreted as testate amoebae, an early example of protists building protective shells. Phosphatic scale microfossils from northwestern Canada suggest that eukaryotes had begun to biomineralise by around 800–720 million years ago, and evidence of eukaryotes preying on other eukaryotes also appears in this interval. Many researchers link the diversification to rising oxygen levels and to the break-up of Rodinia, which created extensive shallow seas along new continental margins.

title: Expanding Earth: a smaller Precambrian planet
summary: Expanding-Earth proponents hold that the Proterozoic planet was far smaller, its surface wholly enclosed by continental crust without deep oceans.
description: The expanding Earth hypothesis, championed in the 20th century by Ott Christoph Hilgenberg and the Australian geologist Samuel Warren Carey of the University of Tasmania, and later by authors such as James Maxlow, proposes that Earth's radius has grown greatly over geological time. In its strongest form, the Precambrian Earth was a fraction of its present size, small enough for all of today's continental crust to fit together into a closed shell with no deep ocean basins. Supercontinents such as Columbia and Rodinia are therefore regarded as unnecessary, with continents simply drifting apart as new ocean floor is added to a swelling globe. Proponents invoke an increase in Earth's mass or a change in its internal state to drive the growth, but have not identified an accepted physical mechanism.
mainstreamView: Plate tectonics explains continental motion without any change in Earth's size: new ocean floor formed at spreading ridges is balanced by crust destroyed at subduction zones, whose sinking slabs seismic imaging traces deep into the mantle. Palaeomagnetic estimates of the ancient radius and satellite geodesy, which finds no statistically significant present-day change in Earth's radius, contradict significant expansion, and no known physics can add the required mass. Proterozoic ophiolites, subduction-related rocks and deep-marine sediments also show that ocean basins and plate boundaries existed throughout the eon.

title: Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event
summary: A second great rise in atmospheric and ocean oxygen helps set the stage for large animals, though its timing and pattern are still debated.
description: Following the low-oxygen Boring Billion, geochemical proxies such as iron speciation, molybdenum and chromium isotopes, and redox-sensitive trace metals indicate a stepwise increase in oxygen during the Neoproterozoic, with the deep ocean becoming persistently oxygenated only around the end of the Ediacaran or later. Proposed drivers include increased burial of organic carbon, nutrients released by weathering of new mountain belts and glacial debris, and the spread of algae. Sections in the Yangtze Gorges area of South China are among the most intensively studied records. It remains unclear whether the increase was a single global event or a series of regional, asynchronous episodes, and how directly it enabled the evolution of animals.

title: Sturtian glaciation: Snowball Earth
summary: Ice sheets reach the equator and may freeze almost the entire ocean surface for some 57 million years, the longest Snowball Earth episode.
description: The Sturtian glaciation, named after glacial deposits along the Sturt River near Adelaide, South Australia, began about 717 million years ago and lasted until about 660 million years ago, opening the Cryogenian Period. Glacial deposits formed at tropical latitudes on many continents, accompanied by the return of banded iron formations, and are overlain by distinctive carbonate layers; Joseph Kirschvink coined the term 'Snowball Earth' in 1992, and Paul Hoffman and colleagues developed the hypothesis in 1998. Proposed triggers include the weathering of vast basalt provinces erupted as Rodinia broke apart, such as the Franklin large igneous province of Arctic Canada, which drew down atmospheric carbon dioxide. High-precision dating shows the onset was nearly synchronous worldwide, and escape from the frozen state is thought to have required volcanic carbon dioxide to build up over millions of years.

title: High-obliquity Earth instead of Snowball Earth
summary: Geologist George Williams argues that a steeply tilted Earth, not a frozen planet, explains why Cryogenian glaciers reached the tropics.
description: Since 1975 the Adelaide-based geologist George E. Williams has argued that Earth's axial tilt, or obliquity, now about 23.4 degrees, exceeded 54 degrees for much of the Precambrian. At such a tilt the equator receives less sunlight over a year than the poles, so ice would form preferentially at low latitudes and seasons would be extreme, which Williams links to signs of strong seasonal freezing and thawing in Cryogenian glacial deposits of South Australia. The idea, later called the HOLIST hypothesis (high obliquity, low-latitude ice, strong seasonality), would explain tropical glaciation without requiring the whole planet to freeze. It requires the tilt to have fallen to modern values around the end of the Precambrian, which Williams and colleagues attributed in 1998 to a feedback between obliquity and the planet's shape.
mainstreamView: The hypothesis is peer-reviewed work by an established geologist, but most researchers reject it. The Moon stabilises Earth's tilt, and studies of tidal and climate-related friction indicate that no known process could have reduced the obliquity from more than 54 degrees to near modern values in the time required. The distribution of Proterozoic evaporites, which form mainly in dry subtropical belts, points to a low obliquity similar to today's, and a tilted Earth does not readily explain the near-synchronous onset of the glaciations, the cap carbonates above them or the return of banded iron formations, which Snowball Earth and its slushball variants account for.

title: Sponge biomarkers: earliest hint of animals?
summary: Steroid molecules characteristic of sponges in Omani rocks older than 635 million years may be the oldest chemical trace of animal life.
description: In 2009 Gordon Love and colleagues reported unusually high abundances of 24-isopropylcholestane, a hydrocarbon derived from sterols made by modern demosponges, in Cryogenian rocks of the Huqf Supergroup drilled in the South Oman Salt Basin. Because these sediments predate the end of the Marinoan glaciation, the finding was interpreted as evidence that sponges, among the earliest-branching animals, existed before about 635 million years ago. That would be tens of millions of years earlier than the oldest widely accepted animal body fossils, but consistent with molecular-clock estimates that place the origin of animals in the Tonian or Cryogenian.
mainstreamView: Many researchers accept the biomarkers as among the best early evidence for animals, but others argue that the same molecules can be produced by certain algae or rhizarian protists, or formed by alteration of other sterols during burial. Unambiguous animal body fossils appear only in the Ediacaran, so the presence of Cryogenian sponges remains unconfirmed.

title: Marinoan glaciation: second Snowball Earth
summary: A second global glaciation ends abruptly 635 million years ago, leaving thick 'cap carbonates' over glacial deposits from Namibia to Australia.
description: The Marinoan glaciation, named after the Adelaide suburb of Marino and also called the Varanger or Elatina glaciation, closed the Cryogenian Period. Its glacial deposits formed near sea level at low latitudes, and in Namibia the Ghaub Formation and its overlying cap carbonate were central to the 1998 Snowball Earth paper by Paul Hoffman and colleagues. Its end, dated to about 635 million years ago, marks the start of the Ediacaran Period and was followed by rapid greenhouse warming, intense weathering and the precipitation of cap carbonates. The onset is poorly constrained, and some recent work suggests the glaciation lasted only a few million years, beginning around 639 million years ago.

title: Pan-African orogeny assembles Gondwana
summary: A network of continental collisions across Africa, South America, Arabia and India welds together the great southern landmass of Gondwana.
description: The Pan-African orogeny comprises a series of Neoproterozoic to early Cambrian mountain-building events in which fragments released by the break-up of Rodinia collided to form Gondwana. Among the largest belts is the East African Orogen, where East and West Gondwana collided along a zone running from the Arabian–Nubian Shield through the Mozambique Belt of Tanzania and Mozambique into Madagascar, India and Antarctica; its South American counterpart is known as the Brasiliano orogeny. Together with the Grenville orogeny, it is one of the two largest known systems of orogenies on Earth. The resulting mountain ranges may have shed large volumes of nutrients into the oceans, a factor sometimes linked to the rise of oxygen and animals.

title: Snowball or slushball? The Cryogenian ice debate
summary: Scientists debate whether Cryogenian oceans froze over completely or kept a belt of open water near the equator in a 'slushball' state.
description: The hard Snowball Earth hypothesis holds that during the Sturtian and Marinoan glaciations sea ice covered almost the entire ocean, shutting down most of the water cycle until volcanic carbon dioxide built up enough greenhouse warming to melt it. Critics have proposed 'slushball' or thin-ice alternatives in which a belt of open or thinly frozen tropical ocean persisted, and some climate models produce a stable state with a narrow equatorial waterway. Evidence of active glaciers, wave-formed sediments and orbitally paced climate cycles within glacial deposits, such as those of the Wilsonbreen Formation in Svalbard, points to a dynamic system with at least some open water. The survival of photosynthetic eukaryotes such as algae through the glaciations, and possibly of early animal lineages, is also cited, since they needed light, open water or other refuges.
mainstreamView: There is broad agreement that ice reached sea level in the tropics during both Cryogenian glaciations. Whether the oceans were almost entirely ice-covered or retained an equatorial strip of open water is unresolved: climate models can produce both states, and many researchers now favour a near-global ice cover punctuated by local open-water refuges and dynamic glaciers.

title: Doushantuo phosphorite fossils
summary: Phosphate deposits at Weng'an, South China, preserve microscopic cell clusters that may include the oldest known animal embryos.
description: The Doushantuo Formation, which spans roughly 635 to 551 million years ago across southern China, contains phosphorites that preserved soft tissue in three dimensions down to the level of individual cells. At Weng'an in Guizhou, vast numbers of tiny spherical fossils divided into 2, 4, 8 and more cells have been interpreted as animal embryos, alongside multicellular algae, acritarchs and possible sponges. The formation also preserves a detailed chemical record of ocean conditions between the Marinoan glaciation and the appearance of the Ediacaran biota. The age of the Weng'an fossils is uncertain, with estimates mostly between about 610 and 580 million years ago.
mainstreamView: The fossils' exceptional preservation is not in question, but their identity is: proposals include animal embryos, non-animal holozoan protists that divide in a similar way, and giant sulfur bacteria. High-resolution X-ray studies of their internal structure have not settled the issue, and many researchers regard the 'embryos' as possible but unconfirmed early animals.

title: Pannotia: a short-lived supercontinent?
summary: Some reconstructions join Gondwana, Laurentia, Baltica and Siberia into a fleeting late-Neoproterozoic supercontinent before the Iapetus Ocean opens.
description: Pannotia ('all southern land'), also called the Vendian supercontinent or Greater Gondwana, was proposed in the 1990s as a supercontinent assembled during the Pan-African and Brasiliano orogenies, when Laurentia lay next to the South American cratons of Amazonia and Río de la Plata. In this model it broke apart around 560 million years ago as the Iapetus Ocean opened between Laurentia, Baltica and Amazonia. The Brasiliano mountain belts of central Brazil mark some of the sutures where its southern components came together. Unlike Rodinia and Pangaea, its very existence is questioned.
mainstreamView: Geologists agree that Gondwana was assembling during the late Neoproterozoic, but many doubt that Laurentia, Baltica and Siberia were ever joined to it at the same time. A 2022 analysis argued that rifting along the Iapetus margins began before Gondwana's assembly was complete, so Pannotia may never have existed as a single landmass.

title: Gaskiers glaciation
summary: A brief ice age lasting only a few hundred thousand years leaves glacial deposits on Newfoundland's Avalon Peninsula and other continents.
description: Named after glaciomarine diamictites packed with dropstones at Gaskiers on Newfoundland's Avalon Peninsula, the Gaskiers glaciation was the last major ice age of the Proterozoic. Uranium–lead dating of volcanic ash beds shows that it lasted only a few hundred thousand years, around 580 million years ago, and deposits attributed to it occur on several palaeocontinents. Unlike the Cryogenian Snowball Earth events, it is not thought to have been global. The oldest large Ediacaran fossils appear in Avalon Peninsula strata a few million years later, prompting suggestions that the end of the glaciation and rising oxygen encouraged the evolution of large organisms.

title: Ediacaran biota: Earth's first large complex life
summary: Large soft-bodied organisms, from fronds to quilted discs and early animals, spread through the oceans in the last 35 million years of the Precambrian.
description: The Ediacaran biota, named after the Ediacara Hills of South Australia where Reg Sprigg found fossils in 1946, are the oldest widespread communities of large, complex multicellular organisms, many big enough to see with the naked eye, although smaller macroscopic algae and other multicellular forms are known from older rocks. They are grouped into three successive assemblages: the deep-water Avalon (about 575–560 million years ago), the diverse shallow-marine White Sea (about 560–550 million years ago) and the Nama (about 550–539 million years ago). Many had body plans unlike any living group, while others such as Kimberella and Dickinsonia are now widely regarded as early animals. Most disappeared by the start of the Cambrian Period, and how they relate to the animals of the Cambrian explosion remains an active area of research.

title: Mistaken Point: oldest complex macrofossils
summary: Deep-sea fossil surfaces in Newfoundland preserve whole communities of frond-like rangeomorphs, among the oldest known large complex organisms.
description: The coastal cliffs of Mistaken Point on the Avalon Peninsula expose bedding planes on which thousands of soft-bodied Ediacaran organisms were smothered in place by volcanic ash, preserving entire seafloor communities from a deep-water setting below the reach of sunlight. Most are rangeomorphs such as Fractofusus, fractally branching organisms from a few centimetres to over a metre long that probably absorbed nutrients directly from seawater, together with stalked fronds such as Charniodiscus. The site also preserves some of the oldest known trace fossils made by mobile organisms, about 565 million years old. Mistaken Point was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016.

title: Shuram excursion: deepest carbon-isotope plunge
summary: Carbonate rocks from Oman to China and Australia record the largest negative carbon-isotope excursion known, a puzzling upheaval in the carbon cycle.
description: Named after the Shuram Formation of Oman, the Shuram excursion is a sharp drop in the carbon-13 content of marine carbonates, with δ13C values falling to around −12‰, well below the roughly −5‰ of carbon released from Earth's mantle. Correlated records have been reported from South Australia's Wonoka Formation, South China's Doushantuo Formation, western North America, Siberia and elsewhere. Rhenium–osmium dating published in 2020 placed it between about 574 and 567 million years ago, although other estimates extend its end to about 560 million years ago or later. Proposed explanations include oxidation of a huge reservoir of dissolved organic carbon in the ocean, release of methane, a surge of sulfate from continental weathering and alteration of the rocks after deposition, and some researchers link it to rising oxygen and the diversification of the Ediacaran biota.
mainstreamView: Most researchers accept that the excursion is recorded on several continents at broadly the same time, but whether it reflects a primary global change in seawater carbon chemistry or was produced or exaggerated by alteration of the carbonates after deposition is still argued over. No single explanation for its unusually low values has been accepted, and how closely it is tied to oxygenation and early animal evolution remains uncertain.

title: Dickinsonia: an Ediacaran animal
summary: Flat, oval, segmented Dickinsonia grows to over a metre long; cholesterol traces in its fossils support its identification as an early animal.
description: Dickinsonia was a thin, oval organism with a central midline and numerous segment-like divisions, ranging from a few millimetres to over a metre in length and found in Australia, Russia, Ukraine, China and elsewhere. It lived on microbial mats on the shallow seafloor, and associated trace fossils suggest that it could move and fed by absorbing nutrients through its underside. For decades it was variously interpreted as a jellyfish, worm, lichen, giant protist or member of an extinct kingdom. In 2018 researchers reported cholesterol-derived biomarkers, characteristic of animals, in organic films of Dickinsonia from cliffs along the White Sea in northern Russia, strengthening its interpretation as an early animal.

title: Kimberella: an early bilaterian grazer
summary: A slug-like animal grazes microbial mats on a seafloor now exposed on Russia's White Sea coast, leaving fan-shaped marks hinting at a mollusc-like mouthpart.
description: Kimberella was first found in South Australia's Ediacara Hills, but hundreds of specimens from the Winter Coast of the White Sea in northern Russia, dated to about 558–555 million years ago, have revealed much more of its anatomy. Up to about 15 cm long, it had a tough, unmineralised dorsal covering and a muscular foot, and is often found at the end of fan-shaped scratch marks (Kimberichnus) made as it grazed microbial mats. Many palaeontologists interpret these features as evidence that Kimberella was a mollusc or a close relative, though this is contested. It is generally accepted as a bilaterian, making it one of the oldest known members of the group that includes most living animals.

title: Ediacaran fossils as land-dwelling lichens
summary: Palaeosol specialist Gregory Retallack argues that Dickinsonia and other Ediacaran fossils were lichens living on land, not marine animals.
description: In a 2013 paper in Nature and later publications, geologist Gregory Retallack argued that red-coloured beds of the Ediacara Member in South Australia's Flinders Ranges are fossil soils rather than marine sediments. On that basis he proposed that many Ediacaran organisms, including Dickinsonia, lived on land and were lichens, fungi or microbial colonies rather than sea creatures. If correct, the hypothesis would mean that large, complex organisms colonised the land far earlier than generally accepted.
mainstreamView: Most sedimentologists interpret the Ediacara Member as shallow-marine deposits shaped by storms and waves, with ripple marks and microbial-mat textures that do not match soils, and attribute the red colour largely to much later weathering. Cholesterol biomarkers preserved in Dickinsonia specimens from Russia point to an animal rather than a lichen. The proposal is peer-reviewed work by an established scientist, but it has been rejected by most palaeontologists.

title: Cloudina and the first animal skeletons
summary: Tiny calcified tubes of Cloudina, built as stacked cones, record one of the earliest animals to grow a mineral skeleton.
description: Cloudina, first described from the Nama Group of southern Namibia and named after geologist Preston Cloud, built millimetre-scale tubes of calcium carbonate made of nested funnels. Along with forms such as Namacalathus, it is among the earliest known biomineralising animals, appearing about 550 million years ago and building reef-like frameworks together with microbial carbonates. Some Cloudina tubes from China bear small round borings, interpreted as among the oldest evidence of predation. Cloudinids are found on several continents, making them a useful marker of the latest Ediacaran, and they disappear near the base of the Cambrian.

title: End-Ediacaran extinction (Kotlin Crisis)
summary: Most Ediacaran organisms vanish in one or two pulses near the end of the Precambrian, clearing the way for the Cambrian explosion.
description: The Ediacaran biota declined sharply near the end of the period: the diverse White Sea assemblage gave way to the less diverse Nama assemblage around 550 million years ago, and most remaining soft-bodied forms and early skeletal organisms disappeared around 539 million years ago. The event is also called the Kotlin Crisis, after the Kotlin Formation near St Petersburg, Russia. Proposed causes include widespread oxygen-poor conditions in the oceans, indicated by uranium isotopes and a sharp negative carbon-isotope excursion near the Ediacaran–Cambrian boundary, and competition from newly evolving burrowing and predatory animals.
mainstreamView: Researchers agree that the Ediacaran biota largely disappeared before or near the start of the Cambrian, but whether this was a true mass extinction or a gradual ecological replacement, and how much of the pattern reflects changes in fossil preservation, is still debated. If confirmed as a mass extinction, it would be the earliest known mass extinction of animals.
